title: Bell Inequalities and Nonlocality
intro: No model in which each particle carries pre-set answers to every question can reproduce the correlations of an entangled pair, and experiments confirm that nature does not. This page derives the CHSH inequality that every such local model must obey, computes the larger value $2\sqrt2$ that a Bell state reaches, and explains what the experiments of 1982 to 2015 did and did not show.

blocks.text: What you need first

Two-qubit states and the tensor product from Composite Systems and Tensor Products (#/quantum/many-body/composite-systems), the Bell states from Entanglement and Reduced States (#/quantum/many-body/entanglement), and expectation values of Pauli operators from Observables and Uncertainty (#/quantum/foundations/observables-and-uncertainty). If you can compute $\langle Z\otimes Z\rangle$ for $\vert00\rangle + \vert11\rangle$, you are ready.
What you will be able to do

items: State Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen's argument, and say exactly what a local hidden variable model is.
Derive the CHSH inequality $\vert S\vert\le2$ for any local model, in three lines of algebra, and check it against all 16 deterministic strategies.
Compute the four correlations of a Bell state for measurement angles of your choice, and show that the best angles give $S = 2\sqrt2$.
Explain what experiments from 1982 to 2015 found, which loopholes they closed, and why none of this lets anyone send a message faster than light.

blocks.text: The puzzle: can the parts of an entangled pair carry their answers with them?
Why we need it

Entanglement was noticed as a worry before it was noticed as a resource. In 1935 Albert Einstein, Boris Podolsky and Nathan Rosen asked whether quantum mechanics could be the whole story. Their argument, restated for qubits, is short, and everything on this page is an attempt to settle it. The surprise is that it can be settled by experiment rather than by taste.
The idea in plain words

Take the Bell state $\vert\Phi^+\rangle = (\vert00\rangle + \vert11\rangle)/\sqrt2$ and send one qubit to Alice and the other to Bob, far away. Three facts about it, each of which you can check with the tools of Observables and Uncertainty (#/quantum/foundations/observables-and-uncertainty):

items: If both measure $Z$ (is the qubit $\vert0\rangle$ or $\vert1\rangle$?), they get the same answer every time, each answer being $+1$ or $-1$ with probability one half.
If both measure $X$, they also get the same answer every time. (Write $\vert\Phi^+\rangle = (\vert{+}{+}\rangle + \vert{-}{-}\rangle)/\sqrt2$: a perfect match in the $\pm$ basis too.)
Alice's single result, taken alone, is a fair coin. Nothing about the state tells her in advance what she will get.

blocks.text: Now Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen reason as follows. Suppose Alice measures $Z$ and gets $+1$. She can then predict, with certainty and without touching Bob's qubit, that Bob would get $+1$ for $Z$. A quantity you can predict with certainty without disturbing the system must correspond to something real about it: call it an element of reality. If Bob's $Z$ answer was real before anyone looked, it was written into Bob's qubit all along. Alice could instead have measured $X$ and predicted Bob's $X$ answer. Her choice, made far away, cannot change Bob's qubit (that is the assumption of locality: no influence travels faster than light). So Bob's qubit must have carried definite answers for both $Z$ and $X$ at once. But a single qubit state $\alpha\vert0\rangle + \beta\vert1\rangle$ has no definite value for both $Z$ and $X$. Hence, they concluded, the quantum state is an incomplete description, and there must be extra variables behind it that fix the answers.

Everyday picture: Bertlmann's socks. If a man always wears one pink and one green sock, then seeing his left sock is pink tells you the right one is green. Nobody thinks the left sock sent a signal. The colours were fixed when he got dressed; the correlation is just shared information. EPR proposed that entangled qubits are like the socks. The picture breaks, as we will see, as soon as there are more than two things you can ask about each qubit.
Local hidden variables, made concrete

Turn the proposal into a precise model that can be tested. A local hidden variable model says: when the pair is created, it is given a shared label $\lambda$ (the hidden variable; it may be one number or a long list, and it may be random with some distribution). After that, each side behaves as follows.

items: Alice, with measurement setting $a$, outputs $A = A(a, \lambda)\in\{+1, -1\}$. It depends on her setting and on $\lambda$, and on nothing else.
Bob, with setting $b$, outputs $B = B(b, \lambda)\in\{+1, -1\}$. It does not depend on Alice's setting $a$ (that is locality).
The settings are chosen freely, independently of $\lambda$ (otherwise the pair could 'know' what will be asked).

blocks.text: Any randomness in a single result is allowed, since it can be hidden in $\lambda$. This is a very general class: it contains every classical way of making correlated answers.

Here is such a model for the two settings $Z$ and $X$. Before each run a coin decides one of four pre-agreed answer sheets, each equally likely; a sheet gives Alice's answers and Bob's answers to both questions.

Each sheet gives Bob the same two answers as Alice. If both ask the same question they always agree, each single answer is a fair coin, and Alice cannot tell which question Bob asked. This reproduces all three facts above exactly. So with only $Z$ and $X$ on the table, EPR's socks work, and nothing quantum is needed. John Bell's insight in 1964 was to ask what happens when Alice and Bob may also choose other directions, such as halfway between $Z$ and $X$. Then the sheets run out of room, and that is what the next sections quantify.

blocks.title: Check yourself: a local model's randomness
blocks.text: In the four-sheet model above, what is the probability that Alice gets $A_Z = +1$, and the probability that Alice and Bob both get $+1$ when both ask $Z$?
blocks.hint: Count the sheets where the answer is $+1$.
solution: Alice's $A_Z$ is $+1$ on sheets 1 and 2, two of the four equally likely sheets: probability $2/4 = 1/2$.
Both get $+1$ when $A_Z = B_Z = +1$, which is also sheets 1 and 2: probability $1/2$. When Alice gets $+1$ Bob always does.

blocks.text: The CHSH inequality: what every local model must obey
Why we need it

To test a whole class of models, not just one, we need a statement that is true for every model in the class and that quantum mechanics can break. John Clauser, Michael Horne, Abner Shimony and Richard Holt found the cleanest one in 1969: it is a single number built from four correlations, and the proof fits in a few lines.
The setup

Alice has two possible settings, $a$ and $a'$, and Bob has two, $b$ and $b'$. On each run each of them picks one setting at random and records a result $\pm1$. After many runs they compare notes and, for each of the four setting pairs, compute the correlation

blocks.tex: E(a, b) = \langle A\,B\rangle = P(\text{same result}) - P(\text{different results})
blocks.caption: The correlation of two ±1 results: +1 means they always agree, −1 always disagree, 0 no relation.

blocks.text: The correlation is the average of the product $AB$: the product is $+1$ when the results agree and $-1$ when they differ. Since the probabilities add to 1, $P(\text{same}) = (1 + E)/2$. Now combine four of them into
The proof for one value of the hidden variable

First suppose the hidden variable has a definite value $\lambda$. Then each of Alice's two possible answers and each of Bob's two possible answers is a definite $\pm1$: write them $A = A(a, \lambda)$, $A' = A(a', \lambda)$, $B = B(b, \lambda)$ and $B' = B(b', \lambda)$. Locality is what allows this: Bob's $B$ and $B'$ do not depend on which of $a$, $a'$ Alice chose, so all four numbers exist together on the same sheet.

items: Step 1. For this $\lambda$, the combination inside the average is $s = AB + AB' + A'B - A'B'$.
Step 2. Group the terms with $A$ and with $A'$: $s = A(B + B') + A'(B - B')$.

Step 3. Each of $B$, $B'$ is $+1$ or $-1$. If $B = B'$, then $B + B' = \pm2$ and $B - B' = 0$. If $B = -B'$, then $B + B' = 0$ and $B - B' = \pm2$. In both cases exactly one bracket is zero and the other is $\pm2$.
Step 4. Since $A$ and $A'$ are also $\pm1$, $s$ equals $\pm2$ times $\pm1$, which is $\pm2$. So $\vert s\vert = 2$ for every $\lambda$.

blocks.text: The table checks this by brute force. There are $2^4 = 16$ ways to fill in $(A, A', B, B')$. A few of them, with the four terms $AB$, $AB'$, $A'B$, $-A'B'$ and their sum:
All 16 give $+2$ or $-2$ (the code below confirms it).
Averaging over hidden variables

A real model has a distribution of hidden variables, with probability $p(\lambda)$ of each. Each correlation is an average over $\lambda$: $E(a, b) = \sum_\lambda p(\lambda)\,A(a, \lambda)B(b, \lambda)$ (an integral if $\lambda$ is continuous). Because averaging is linear, $S = \sum_\lambda p(\lambda)\,s(\lambda)$, an average of numbers that are each $+2$ or $-2$. An average of numbers between $-2$ and $2$ stays between them:

blocks.caption: The CHSH inequality: every local hidden variable model obeys it.

blocks.text: Notice how little was assumed: nothing about how $\lambda$ is produced, how many values it takes, or what physics makes the answers. Only two things were used: the answers are fixed by $\lambda$ and the local setting, and the settings are chosen independently of $\lambda$.

A common confusion: the inequality is not about one run. A single run gives four numbers, but only one of the four correlations is touched on each run, because Alice and Bob each use one setting. The four correlations come from four different groups of runs. The proof says that the sheets could not have been filled in to give a larger average, even though no run reveals a full sheet.

blocks.title: Check yourself: a classical strategy
blocks.text: A local model has $A = +1$ and $A' = -1$ always, and Bob answers $B = +1$, $B' = -1$ always. What is $S$?
blocks.hint: Compute the four products first, then $S = E(a,b) + E(a,b') + E(a',b) - E(a',b')$.
solution: So $S = -2$, not $+2$; the bound is on $\vert S\vert$ and both signs occur. (Flipping Bob's answers, $B = -1$, $B' = +1$, gives $+2$.)

blocks.text: What quantum mechanics predicts: S = 2√2
Why we need it
If quantum mechanics also obeyed $\vert S\vert\le2$, there would be nothing to test. So we compute what a Bell state gives for the same four settings, and look for angles where it beats 2.
Measuring along an angle
Each party measures a spin-like quantity along a direction in the $xz$ plane of the Bloch sphere, at angle $\theta$ from the $z$ axis. The observable is

blocks.caption: Measuring the qubit along the direction at angle θ in the xz-plane of the Bloch sphere; results ±1.

blocks.text: It has eigenvalues $\pm1$ (it is a Pauli-type matrix: its square is $\cos^2\theta\,I + \sin^2\theta\,I + \cos\theta\sin\theta\,(ZX + XZ) = I$, because $ZX + XZ = 0$). At $\theta = 0$ it is $Z$ and at $\theta = \pi/2$ it is $X$. Its $+1$ eigenvector is $\cos(\theta/2)\vert0\rangle + \sin(\theta/2)\vert1\rangle$, the state at polar angle $\theta$ on the Bloch sphere (The Qubit and the Bloch Sphere (#/quantum/qubits/bloch-sphere)). For photons, where the qubit is polarisation, the angle $\theta$ corresponds to a polariser turned by $\theta/2$, so settings of $\theta = 0$, $\pi/2$ are polarisers at $0°$ and $45°$.
The correlation in a Bell state

Alice uses angle $\alpha$ on qubit 1 and Bob uses angle $\beta$ on qubit 2. The joint observable is $\sigma(\alpha)\otimes\sigma(\beta)$, and its average in $\vert\Phi^+\rangle = (\vert00\rangle + \vert11\rangle)/\sqrt2$ is the correlation $E(\alpha, \beta)$. Expand the product of the two sums:
Now take the average of each Pauli product in $\vert\Phi^+\rangle$, one at a time.

items: Step 1. $Z\otimes Z$ gives $+1$ on $\vert00\rangle$ and $+1$ on $\vert11\rangle$ (two minus signs make a plus). So $Z\otimes Z\,\vert\Phi^+\rangle = \vert\Phi^+\rangle$ and $\langle Z\otimes Z\rangle = 1$.

Step 2. $X\otimes X$ swaps $\vert0\rangle\leftrightarrow\vert1\rangle$ on both qubits: $\vert00\rangle\to\vert11\rangle$ and $\vert11\rangle\to\vert00\rangle$. So $X\otimes X\,\vert\Phi^+\rangle = \vert\Phi^+\rangle$ and $\langle X\otimes X\rangle = 1$.

Step 3. $Z\otimes X$ turns $\vert00\rangle$ into $\vert01\rangle$ and $\vert11\rangle$ into $-\vert10\rangle$. The result, $(\vert01\rangle - \vert10\rangle)/\sqrt2$, is orthogonal to $\vert\Phi^+\rangle$, so $\langle Z\otimes X\rangle = 0$. In the same way $\langle X\otimes Z\rangle = 0$.
Step 4. Put the four averages into the expansion: $E(\alpha, \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + \sin\alpha\sin\beta = \cos(\alpha - \beta)$, by the cosine subtraction formula.

blocks.caption: Correlation of two angle measurements on the Bell state |Φ⁺⟩: it depends only on the difference of the angles.

blocks.text: Sanity checks. Equal angles give $E = 1$ (perfect agreement, as in the facts at the start). Angles differing by $\pi/2$, such as $Z$ for Alice and $X$ for Bob, give $E = 0$: no relation. Angles differing by $\pi$ give $E = -1$: perfect disagreement. In between the correlation varies smoothly like a cosine; the probability that the two results agree is $(1 + \cos(\alpha - \beta))/2 = \cos^2\left(\frac{\alpha - \beta}{2}\right)$. A local model cannot reproduce a smooth cosine in all four places; that is the point of the next steps.
Choosing the angles

Choose Alice's two angles $a = 0$ and $a' = \pi/2$ (that is, $Z$ and $X$), and Bob's two angles $b = \pi/4$ and $b' = -\pi/4$ (the directions halfway between $Z$ and $X$, on either side). Every difference of an Alice angle and a Bob angle is then an odd multiple of $\pi/4$.

blocks.caption: A Bell state beats the classical bound by 41%.

blocks.text: There it is: a number the local model is forbidden to reach. In terms of probabilities, for $E = 0.7071$ the two results agree with probability $(1 + 0.7071)/2 = 0.8536$ for the first three setting pairs, and agree only $(1 - 0.7071)/2 = 0.1464$ of the time for the last. No assignment of answer sheets can do that.

A second way to see the same number, without choosing angles by hand: add Alice's two terms with Bob's operator. For these angles $\sigma(b) + \sigma(b') = \sqrt2\,Z$ and $\sigma(b) - \sigma(b') = \sqrt2\,X$ (the $X$ parts cancel in the sum, the $Z$ parts in the difference). So the operator $S = Z\otimes(\sigma(b) + \sigma(b')) + X\otimes(\sigma(b) - \sigma(b')) = \sqrt2\,(Z\otimes Z + X\otimes X)$. In $\vert\Phi^+\rangle$ both $Z\otimes Z$ and $X\otimes X$ equal $+1$, so $S = \sqrt2(1 + 1) = 2\sqrt2$. This is the classical proof's step 2 with operators in place of numbers; the two perfect correlations $Z\otimes Z$ and $X\otimes X$ add up to more than the $\pm2$ that numbers allow.
Why 2√2 and not more

Can other states or angles do better? Not for quantum mechanics: Boris Tsirelson showed in 1980 that $2\sqrt2$ is the maximum. Here is the short derivation. Let $A$, $A'$ (on Alice's qubit) and $B$, $B'$ (on Bob's) be any observables with eigenvalues $\pm1$, so each squares to the identity, and Alice's operators commute with Bob's. Expand $S^2$ for $S = AB + AB' + A'B - A'B'$. The four squared terms give $4I$ (for example $(AB)^2 = A^2B^2 = I$). The cross terms $AB\cdot AB' + AB'\cdot AB = BB' + B'B$ cancel against $-(A'B\,A'B' + A'B'\,A'B) = -(BB' + B'B)$, and $AB\cdot A'B + A'B\cdot AB = AA' + A'A$ cancels against the matching terms with $-A'B'$. What remains is

Each commutator is at most 2 in size: $[A, A'] = AA' - A'A$, and a product of two $\pm1$ observables never stretches a vector, so each term has size at most 1. Hence $[A, A'][B, B']$ has size at most $4$, and $S^2\le4 + 4 = 8$, so $\vert S\vert\le2\sqrt2$. For our angles $[A, A'] = [Z, X] = 2iY$ on qubit 1 and $[B, B'] = -2iY$ on qubit 2, so $S^2 = 4I - (2iY)\otimes(-2iY) = 4I - 4\,Y\otimes Y$. On $\vert\Phi^+\rangle$ we have $\langle Y\otimes Y\rangle = -1$ (the three Bell-state parities multiply to $-1$, as shown on Commutators and Compatible Observables (#/quantum/foundations/commutators)), so $S^2 = 4 + 4 = 8$ and the bound is reached. Notice the key ingredient: $[A, A']\ne0$. If Alice's two observables commuted, there would be no extra $-[A, A'][B, B']$ term and $S^2\le4$, back to the classical bound. The violation comes from Alice's two settings being incompatible questions (Commutators and Compatible Observables (#/quantum/foundations/commutators)), which classical sheets of answers assume are all answerable at once.
Check it with numbers

The program below builds the observables $\sigma(\theta)$ as matrices, computes the four correlations in $\vert\Phi^+\rangle$ with the tensor product, and then runs the classical side: it lists $S$ for all 16 deterministic strategies, tests the best classical model that uses a shared random angle, and finally simulates 20000 runs per setting pair with random outcomes drawn from the quantum probabilities, the way an experiment would. The last block anticipates the section on signalling below.

blocks.source:
from itertools import product
import numpy as np

# Pauli matrices and the Bell state |Phi+> = (|00> + |11>)/sqrt(2)
X = np.array([[0, 1], [1, 0]], dtype=float)
Z = np.diag([1.0, -1.0])
phi = np.array([1, 0, 0, 1]) / np.sqrt(2)

def spin(angle):
    """Observable cos(angle) Z + sin(angle) X: measure the spin along a direction in the xz-plane."""
    return np.cos(angle) * Z + np.sin(angle) * X

def E(a, b):
    """Correlation <A(a) (x) B(b)> in |Phi+>: Alice's observable on qubit 1, Bob's on qubit 2."""
    return phi @ np.kron(spin(a), spin(b)) @ phi

def eigvecs(t):
    """Eigenvectors of spin(t): outcome +1 then outcome -1."""
    return [np.array([np.cos(t/2), np.sin(t/2)]), np.array([-np.sin(t/2), np.cos(t/2)])]

def joint(sa, sb):
    """P(Alice outcome, Bob outcome) for settings sa, sb, as a dict keyed by (+-1, +-1)."""
    out = {}
    for i, va in enumerate(eigvecs(sa)):
        for j, vb in enumerate(eigvecs(sb)):
            out[(1 - 2*i, 1 - 2*j)] = (np.kron(va, vb) @ phi) ** 2
    return out

a, a2 = 0.0, np.pi / 2            # Alice's two settings
b, b2 = np.pi / 4, -np.pi / 4     # Bob's two settings
pairs = {"E(a,b)": (a, b), "E(a,b')": (a, b2), "E(a',b)": (a2, b), "E(a',b')": (a2, b2)}
corr = {}
for name, (sa, sb) in pairs.items():
    corr[name] = E(sa, sb)
    print(f"{name:9s} = {corr[name]:+.4f}   cos(angle difference) = {np.cos(sa - sb):+.4f}")
S = corr["E(a,b)"] + corr["E(a,b')"] + corr["E(a',b)"] - corr["E(a',b')"]
print(f"quantum S = {S:.4f}   2*sqrt(2) = {2*np.sqrt(2):.4f}")

# Classical bound: every deterministic strategy (A, A', B, B' all +-1) gives |S| = 2
vals = sorted({A*B + A*B2 + A2*B - A2*B2 for A, A2, B, B2 in product([1, -1], repeat=4)})
print("S over all 16 deterministic strategies:", vals)

# Best local model with a shared random angle: both answer sign(cos(setting - lam))
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
lam = rng.uniform(0, 2*np.pi, 400_000)
ans = lambda s: np.sign(np.cos(s - lam))
Elhv = lambda s, t: np.mean(ans(s) * ans(t))
S_lhv = Elhv(a, b) + Elhv(a, b2) + Elhv(a2, b) - Elhv(a2, b2)
print(f"shared-angle local model: E(a,b) = {Elhv(a, b):+.3f}, S = {S_lhv:.3f}  (sawtooth 1-2|a-b|/pi, not cosine)")

# Finite shots: sample the two outcomes from the quantum probabilities
def sample_E(sa, sb, shots=20000):
    p = joint(sa, sb)
    keys = list(p)
    draws = rng.choice(len(keys), size=shots, p=[p[k] for k in keys])
    return np.mean([keys[d][0] * keys[d][1] for d in draws])
Es = [sample_E(*pairs[n]) for n in pairs]
S_shots = Es[0] + Es[1] + Es[2] - Es[3]
print("sampled E:", np.round(Es, 3), f" S from 4 x 20000 shots = {S_shots:.3f}  (standard error about 0.01)")

# No signalling: Bob's outcome statistics do not depend on Alice's setting
for sa in (a, a2, 1.0):
    p = joint(sa, b)
    print(f"Alice setting {sa:.2f}: P(Bob = +1) = {p[(1, 1)] + p[(-1, 1)]:.4f},  P(Alice = +1) = {p[(1, 1)] + p[(1, -1)]:.4f},  P(both +1) = {p[(1, 1)]:.4f}")

blocks.text: Output of the run: the four correlations are $+0.7071$, $+0.7071$, $+0.7071$ and $-0.7071$, each equal to the cosine of the angle difference, and $S = 2.8284$. Over the 16 deterministic strategies $S$ takes only the values $-2$ and $2$. A local model in which the pair shares a random angle $\lambda$ and each side answers $\mathrm{sign}\cos(\text{setting} - \lambda)$, gets $S = 2.000$ at these settings, right at the classical limit: its correlation is a straight-line sawtooth $1 - 2\vert\alpha - \beta\vert/\pi$ (which is $0.5$ at an angle difference of $\pi/4$) where quantum mechanics has the cosine ($0.7071$). Simulating 20000 runs per setting pair, with outcomes drawn from the quantum probabilities, gives $S = 2.830$ with a standard error of about $0.01$: a violation of the bound by some 80 standard errors.

blocks.text: Alice measures along $\theta = 0$ and Bob along $\theta = \pi/3$ on $\vert\Phi^+\rangle$. What is the correlation, and how often do their results agree?
blocks.answer: E = 0.5; they agree 75% of the time

blocks.text: What experiments found
Why we need it

A violation on paper proves nothing about nature. The test is whether real pairs of particles, measured with real detectors, produce $\vert S\vert > 2$ under conditions where a local model would have had no way to cheat. Making that rigorous took half a century, because each experiment leaves a gap (a 'loophole') through which a local model could in principle still live.
The three loopholes

items: The locality loophole. If Alice's setting choice and result could be known at Bob's station before Bob finishes, signals at light speed (or slower) could coordinate their answers, and the proof's assumption that $B$ does not depend on $a$ fails. To close it, the two measurements (choosing the setting and recording the result) must be so close in time and so far apart that light has no time to cross between them.

The detection loophole. Real detectors miss many particles. If only a small fraction of pairs are detected, a local model can arrange that the detected pairs are an unrepresentative subset that appears to violate the inequality, even though the full ensemble would not. Closing it needs high enough detection efficiency overall: for equal detectors on both sides and no background counts, above $2/(1+\sqrt2)\approx83\%$ for the CHSH test with a maximally entangled state, and above about two thirds (a result of Philippe Eberhard, 1993) when a suitably chosen less-entangled state and a matching inequality are used.

The freedom-of-choice loophole. The proof assumes the setting is chosen independently of $\lambda$. If settings were fixed by something correlated with the hidden variable, the bound could fail. Experiments make the choice with fast random-number generators or the light of distant stars; no experiment can exclude a conspiracy stretching back to the Big Bang, but they can push it ever further out.

blocks.text: The experiments

Alain Aspect, Philippe Grangier and Gérard Roger reported tests with entangled photon pairs from calcium atoms in 1981 and, with Jean Dalibard, in 1982 (Aspect, Dalibard and Roger, Physical Review Letters 49, 1804). In the 1982 experiment each photon met a fast optical switch that sent it to one of two polarisers set at different orientations, so each side's setting was changed while the photons were in flight, faster than light could cross the roughly 12 metres between the two sides. The switching followed a regular (quasi-periodic) pattern rather than a random one, and the detectors missed most photons, so the locality loophole was only partly closed and the detection loophole not at all; but the inequality was violated and the quantum prediction confirmed. Further experiments closed one loophole at a time.

In 2015 three groups closed the detection and locality loopholes in the same experiment. Hensen and coworkers in Delft entangled two electron spins in diamond defects (nitrogen-vacancy centres) 1.3 kilometres apart; spins can be read out with very high efficiency, so detection was no problem, and the distance gave the locality closure. In 245 trials they found $S = 2.42\pm0.20$; the chance of a local model producing a violation at least that large was estimated at about $4\%$ ($p = 0.039$), a real but modest margin. Giustina and coworkers in Vienna, and Shalm and coworkers at NIST in Boulder, used entangled photons with superconducting detectors efficient enough to close the detection loophole, fast random setting choices and enough separation to close the locality loophole too. These two photon experiments tested a form of the inequality designed for imperfect detectors (the Clauser-Horne form with Eberhard's choice of state) rather than CHSH itself, and reached far stronger statistical significance: the Vienna group quotes a probability below $10^{-30}$ for local realism to produce their data, and the NIST group about $10^{-7}$. The 2022 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Alain Aspect, John Clauser and Anton Zeilinger for experiments with entangled photons that established the violation of Bell inequalities and opened the way to quantum information science.

Be careful about what 'loophole-free' means. It means that the specific known gaps (locality, detection, and with random enough settings a large part of freedom of choice) are closed in one run of the experiment. It does not mean the interpretation is settled; it means that the simplest family of classical explanations, local hidden variables, has been tested directly and has failed.
What it means, and what it does not
Why we need it

Bell violations are often described as 'spooky action at a distance' or 'faster-than-light influence'. These phrases are misleading in a specific way, and getting them right is part of understanding the result.
What is ruled out

Every local hidden variable model satisfies $\vert S\vert\le2$, and nature does not. So nature is not described by any model in which (1) each measurement has a definite pre-existing result fixed by a shared variable plus the local setting, (2) nothing at Alice's station affects Bob's result, and (3) the settings are free. At least one of the three must go. Physicists differ about which. Giving up locality gives theories such as Bohmian mechanics, where the hidden variables (positions) are influenced instantaneously across space. Giving up the single definite outcome gives the many-worlds reading. Giving up free settings gives superdeterminism. Standard quantum mechanics says only that the predictions are correct and does not pick.
What is not shown: no signalling

None of these lets Alice send Bob a message. The reason is a short calculation that you can run on the Bell state. If Alice measures along angle $\alpha$ and Bob along $\beta$, the probability of each pair of results is $P(s, t) = \tfrac14\left(1 + s\,t\cos(\alpha - \beta)\right)$ for $s, t = \pm1$. Add over Alice's two results to get what Bob sees on his own:

blocks.caption: Summing over Alice's result removes the cosine, whatever her setting.

blocks.text: The first term is for Alice's result $s = +1$ and the second for $s = -1$; the cosines cancel. Bob's results are a fair coin whatever Alice does, including whether she measures at all, so he receives no information. The last line of the program above checks this: for three different settings of Alice, $P(\text{Bob} = +1) = 0.5000$, while the joint probability of both getting $+1$ changes with her setting ($0.4268$ for the first two, $0.4943$ for the third). The correlation lives in the joint statistics, and joint statistics exist only once the two records are brought together, by an ordinary classical message.

There is a general version. Bob's qubit is described by the reduced state obtained by tracing out Alice's qubit (The Partial Trace and Reduced States (#/quantum/many-body/partial-trace)). Anything Alice does on her side, a measurement with the result kept or thrown away, changes the joint state but leaves Bob's reduced state alone. For a measurement with projectors $\Pi_k$ whose results are discarded, the new joint state is $\sum_k(\Pi_k\otimes I)\rho(\Pi_k\otimes I)$. Tracing out Alice's qubit, a factor that acts on Alice's qubit only can be moved cyclically around the partial trace (just as in an ordinary trace), so the right-hand $\Pi_k\otimes I$ meets the left-hand one and $\Pi_k^2 = \Pi_k$. That gives $\operatorname{Tr}_A\sum_k(\Pi_k\otimes I)\rho(\Pi_k\otimes I) = \operatorname{Tr}_A\sum_k(\Pi_k\otimes I)\rho = \operatorname{Tr}_A\left(\left(\sum_k\Pi_k\right)\otimes I\,\rho\right) = \operatorname{Tr}_A\rho$ since the projectors add to the identity. So Bob's statistics are untouched. This property, that local actions cannot change the other side's statistics, is called no-signalling, and quantum mechanics obeys it exactly.
Other things people get wrong

items: Entanglement is not the same as violating Bell: states that are entangled but too noisy to beat 2 exist. A mixture $v\,\vert\Phi^+\rangle\langle\Phi^+\vert + (1 - v)\,I/4$ (a Bell state with a fraction $1 - v$ of pure noise) has correlations scaled by $v$, because the noise term has zero correlations. So $S = 2\sqrt2\,v$, which exceeds 2 only if $v > 1/\sqrt2 = 0.7071$. Noise (Mixed States (#/quantum/many-body/mixed-states) and Decoherence: How Superpositions Fade (#/quantum/many-body/decoherence)) kills the violation before it kills the entanglement.
A Bell violation is a property of the observed data: it certifies entanglement and genuine randomness without trusting the devices, which is why it underlies device-independent cryptography.

blocks.title: Check yourself: noise and the Bell test
blocks.text: A source makes the state $v\,\vert\Phi^+\rangle\langle\Phi^+\vert + (1 - v)\,I/4$ with $v = 0.9$. What is $S$ for the angles used above? Is the inequality violated?
solution: The identity part has zero correlation for any observables $\sigma(\alpha)\otimes\sigma(\beta)$, since $\operatorname{Tr}(\sigma(\alpha)\otimes\sigma(\beta)) = 0$; only the Bell part contributes, scaled by $v$.

blocks.text: Putting it together

The CHSH game packages the test as a game. A referee gives Alice a random bit $x$ and Bob a random bit $y$, they answer $\pm1$ without talking, and they win if $A\,B = +1$ whenever $(x, y)\ne(1, 1)$ and $A\,B = -1$ when $(x, y) = (1, 1)$. Find the best winning probability for classical strategies, and for the Bell state.

items: Step 1. Identify the game with CHSH: let $x = 0$ choose $a$, $x = 1$ choose $a'$, and $y = 0$ choose $b$, $y = 1$ choose $b'$. Winning means $AB = +1$ for the settings pairs $(a, b)$, $(a, b')$, $(a', b)$ and $AB = -1$ for $(a', b')$: the same sign pattern as in $S$.

Step 2. Write the probability of winning as an average over the four equally likely setting pairs: $P_{\text{win}} = \tfrac14\left[\tfrac{1 + E(a,b)}{2} + \tfrac{1 + E(a,b')}{2} + \tfrac{1 + E(a',b)}{2} + \tfrac{1 - E(a',b')}{2}\right]$.
Step 3. Add up: $P_{\text{win}} = \tfrac14\cdot\tfrac{4 + S}{2} = \tfrac12 + \tfrac{S}{8}$.

Step 4. Classically $S\le2$, so $P_{\text{win}}\le\tfrac12 + \tfrac28 = 0.75$. (Check by hand: a fixed strategy can win at most 3 of the 4 pairs, since the product of the four target signs is $-1$ while the product of the four actual signs $AB\cdot AB'\cdot A'B\cdot A'B' = (AA'BB')^2 = +1$; so at least one pair always loses.)
Step 5. With the Bell state, $S = 2\sqrt2$, so $P_{\text{win}} = \tfrac12 + \tfrac{2\sqrt2}{8} = \tfrac12 + \tfrac{\sqrt2}{4} = 0.8536$. This equals $\cos^2(\pi/8)$.

Step 6. So the quantum pair wins about $85.4\%$ of the time against a classical ceiling of $75\%$, with no communication during the game. With noise $v = 0.9$ (the check above), $S = 2.546$ and $P_{\text{win}} = 0.5 + 2.546/8 = 0.818$.

blocks.text: Key points

items: EPR argued that perfect correlations mean the answers were pre-existing, so quantum mechanics is incomplete; Bell turned this into a testable claim by allowing more than two settings.
A local hidden variable model gives each side an answer fixed by a shared $\lambda$ and its own setting; Bob's answer does not depend on Alice's setting, and settings are free.
For any such model, $S = E(a, b) + E(a, b') + E(a', b) - E(a', b')$ obeys $\vert S\vert\le2$, because $A(B + B') + A'(B - B') = \pm2$ for every sheet of answers.

For the Bell state $\vert\Phi^+\rangle$, $E(\alpha, \beta) = \cos(\alpha - \beta)$; angles $0$, $\pi/2$ for Alice and $\pm\pi/4$ for Bob give $S = 2\sqrt2$, the maximum quantum mechanics allows (Tsirelson).
The violation needs Alice's two observables not to commute: $S^2 = 4I - [A, A'][B, B']$.
Experiments from 1982 to the loophole-free tests of 2015 find the violation; the three loopholes are locality, detection and freedom of choice.
No-signalling holds: Bob's statistics do not depend on what Alice does, so no message is sent; the correlation appears only when records are compared.
Noise reduces $S$ in proportion to the lost correlation: $S = 2\sqrt2\,v$ for a Bell state mixed with white noise.

blocks.text: Problems

blocks.title: The singlet
blocks.text: The singlet state is $\vert\Psi^-\rangle = (\vert01\rangle - \vert10\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Find $\langle Z\otimes Z\rangle$ and $\langle X\otimes X\rangle$, write the correlation $E(\alpha, \beta)$ for the measurements $\sigma(\alpha)\otimes\sigma(\beta)$, and compute $S$ for the angles used on this page.
blocks.hint: Compute the action of $Z\otimes Z$ and $X\otimes X$ on $\vert01\rangle$ and $\vert10\rangle$.
solution: $Z\otimes Z$ is $-1$ on both $\vert01\rangle$ and $\vert10\rangle$ (the bits differ), so $\langle Z\otimes Z\rangle = -1$.

$X\otimes X\,\vert01\rangle = \vert10\rangle$ and $X\otimes X\,\vert10\rangle = \vert01\rangle$, so $X\otimes X\,\vert\Psi^-\rangle = (\vert10\rangle - \vert01\rangle)/\sqrt2 = -\vert\Psi^-\rangle$ and $\langle X\otimes X\rangle = -1$.

$\langle Z\otimes X\rangle = \langle X\otimes Z\rangle = 0$ (the result is orthogonal to the singlet, as for $\vert\Phi^+\rangle$), so $E(\alpha, \beta) = -\cos\alpha\cos\beta - \sin\alpha\sin\beta = -\cos(\alpha - \beta)$.

Every correlation of the page is therefore reversed in sign: $-0.7071$, $-0.7071$, $-0.7071$, $+0.7071$, and $S = -2\sqrt2 = -2.828$. The size is the same, so $\vert S\vert = 2\sqrt2$ and the violation is the same.

blocks.title: A different set of angles
blocks.text: With Alice at $a = 0$, $a' = \pi/2$ and Bob at $b = \pi/3$, $b' = -\pi/3$ on $\vert\Phi^+\rangle$, compute $S$. Is it a violation?
solution: $S = 0.5 + 0.5 + 0.8660 + 0.8660 = 2.732$. Yes, a violation, though below the maximum $2.828$. (Equivalently $S = 2\cos(\pi/3) + 2\sin(\pi/3) = 1 + 1.732$.)

blocks.title: The Bell state through a dephasing channel
blocks.text: Qubit 1 of $\vert\Phi^+\rangle$ suffers dephasing that multiplies every off-diagonal element of its density matrix by $c = 0.5$ (Decoherence: How Superpositions Fade (#/quantum/many-body/decoherence) shows where this comes from). Then $\langle Z\otimes Z\rangle$ stays $1$ while $\langle X\otimes X\rangle$ becomes $c$ and the correlation is $E(\alpha, \beta) = \cos\alpha\cos\beta + c\sin\alpha\sin\beta$. Compute $S$ for the page's angles and the smallest $c$ that still violates with these angles.
blocks.hint: Substitute the angles into the new $E$; the $\sin0$ and $\cos\tfrac\pi2$ terms vanish.
solution: $S > 2$ needs $1 + c > 1.4142$, i.e. $c > 0.4142$. Below that, these angles give no violation (other angles can do slightly better: the best possible is $2\sqrt{1 + c^2}$, which exceeds 2 for any $c > 0$).

blocks.text: Where this is used

items: The reason noise matters so much for entanglement, and how an environment erases it: Decoherence: How Superpositions Fade (#/quantum/many-body/decoherence).

Describing the state of one half of an entangled pair, and the mixed states that arise: Mixed States (#/quantum/many-body/mixed-states) and The Partial Trace and Reduced States (#/quantum/many-body/partial-trace).
Correlations between qubits are the raw material of a quantum reservoir's features: Spin Models (#/quantum/many-body/spin-models).
Bell violation as a certificate of entanglement without trusting devices: the basis of device-independent quantum key distribution and randomness certification (see Brunner et al. below).
